title: Four Lines Of Denial
meaning: Someone asked what God is made of, and this surah answers in four lines that each take something away. God is one, in a word Arabic uses for nothing else here. He is the one everyone turns to, and He needs nothing from anyone. He did not father anyone and no one fathered Him, which closes both directions of descent at once. And nothing is equal to Him. Notice what the surah never does: it never says what God is like. The early scholars treat that silence as the point.
historicalContext: This surah came down in Mecca, and the sources say it was an answer. People had asked the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to describe his Lord: what He was made of, and who His ancestors were. The reports differ over who asked, but not over the question. In Arabia the gods had family lines and home ground, so a question about lineage was the first one anyone would put to a new claim about God.

keyTerms.note: Not the ordinary word for the number one. Arabic uses it in negative sentences to mean not anyone at all. Used here in a positive one, it says a oneness with no second of any kind.
The root means to head toward a thing, and also to be solid with nothing hollow inside. Early scholars keep both: the one everyone turns to in need, and the one with nothing empty in Him.
The word for a marriage partner of matching standing, and for anything of equal worth. Denying it removes rivals and peers alike. No scale is left on which to make the comparison.

lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian gods were family. The three named in another surah were called daughters of a higher god. Shrines passed from father to son, and a god belonged to one place and one people. Asking about a god's parents was not rude. It was how you found out whose god it was. The third line answers by refusing the whole idea.
didYouKnow: The early collections keep a report that this surah is worth a third of the Quran. Another says a man repeated it all night, and was told his love for it would bring him into the garden. It is four short lines. The old explanation of the sum is that the Quran's subject matter falls into three parts, and this is one of them.
theologicalSignificance: Describing God by denial stops the description turning into a picture. That is the surah's whole method. Any positive image a person forms is borrowed from something made. Each line here removes one such image before it can settle. What is left cannot be pictured, and a child can still recite it. So it became the shortest full answer in the tradition.

crossReferences.why: Denies any likeness in the same way, then hangs two attributes on that denial in one line.
Uses the same method at greater length, saying what God is not rather than drawing a picture.
Answers the same claim about descent at length, with the heavens near to splitting at it.

applyIt: Say these four lines once, and then notice what picture your mind supplied anyway. Everyone supplies one: a light, a direction, a presence somewhere above. Do not fight it. The surah works by removing pictures one at a time, and you cannot remove a picture you have not caught yourself making.
explainEasier: God is one. He is not made of anything. He has no father and no children. No one is like Him at all. Everyone needs Him for what they need, and He needs no one.
